title: Orchid Systems - interconnect and egress evaluation
summary: Initial discovery focused on how Redwood Private can fit within Orchid's strict no-internet-egress policy, cross-region traffic constraints, and existing DirectConnect/ExpressRoute hybrid network. Key asks: VPC peering vs private endpoints, egress IP controls, management plane connectivity, and a simple benchmark plan.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-11-18 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Li (Redwood AE), Priya Raman (Redwood SE), Carlos Mendes (Redwood Solutions Eng), Maya Torres (Orchid Head of Infra), Samir Patel (Platform Eng), Lena Chu (Security Architect), Evan Brooks (DevOps)

Summary (auto): quick discovery about private deployment network patterns, strict egress/no-internet requirement, and idea for a small pilot to test peering + fixed egress IP.

[00:00] Jordan Li: Hey everyone, thanks for making time. Quick round robin? who wants to start, Maya?
[00:10] Maya Torres: Sure, yeah, I'll kick off. We run Orchids platform across us-east-1 and eu-west-1. We're in the middle of consolidating a bunch of models behind a single inference plane. Primary constraint is, we cannot have uncontrolled internet egress — everything must go through approved endpoints.
[00:28] Samir Patel: And we have a couple of DirectConnects for our colo, plus some ExpressRoute to Azure for EU tenants. We wanna know how Redwood Private would peer with us and what outbound IPs we can lock to.
[00:41] Priya Raman: Got it, thanks. For context, Redwood Private can be deployed into a customer-managed VPC (or a VPC we provision under customer account) and we support both VPC peering and private endpoints depending on cloud and region. The management plane needs limited outbound connectivity for control signals, but data plane traffic can be entirely internal if you choose peering or private endpoints.
[01:05] Lena Chu: Is there any component that requires internet outbound for updates or telemetry? Our security policy disallows any egress to internet except to a handful of corporate destinations.
[01:18] Carlos Mendes: Good question. The control plane by default talks to Redwood's hosted control plane for orchestrations, but we have a Private-mode option where the control plane can be run in a customer VPC or via a customer-managed NAT with strict allowlist. We also support VPC endpoints for S3/KMS/logging, so you can avoid internet egress for artifacts and metrics. (brief chuckle) Not magically, but with the right endpoints it's doable.
[01:44] Evan Brooks: So concretely—if we want zero internet egress, is the path: set up VPC peering to Redwood nodes in our account or do private endpoints? Which is simpler?
[01:56] Priya Raman: Simpler depends on scale. For a single-region pilot, private endpoints (AWS PrivateLink, GCP Private Service Connect) are quick: you get a stable ENI and traffic never leaves AWS backbone. For multi-region or cross-account heavy traffic, peering or Transit Gateway style attachments give higher throughput and simpler routing but require route table edits and careful CIDR planning.
[02:21] Maya Torres: Our VPC CIDRs are kind of ugly (overlapping ranges with a few partners), so peering might hit us. We already use a Transit Gateway for east-west; can Redwood attach to our TGW?
[02:33] Jordan Li: Yes, we can attach to Transit Gateway in AWS. We usually recommend TGW for customers with many VPCs since it centralizes routes. We'll share a TGW attachment guide — it's part of the peering cookbook.
[02:45] Samir Patel: Ok — and what about fixed egress IPs? Our compliance team wants a set of static outbound IP ranges for allowlisting in partner services.
[02:56] Priya Raman: For egress, two patterns: 1) You route through your NAT/egress gateways — then the egress IPs are yours and stable; or 2) if Redwood manages egress in our dedicated deployment, we can provide stable egress IPs as part of a dedicated reserved pool. For Private (customer VPC) we recommend using your own NAT or an egress appliance so you keep control.
[03:20] Lena Chu: So we could insist that all outbound to S3/KMS/logging goes via our VPC endpoints, and all other destinations are blocked. That good?
[03:29] Carlos Mendes: Yep. We also support configuring the runtime to only write logs to your collector via a VPC endpoint. Audit events can be delivered to your Kinesis or PubSub inside your network.
[03:39] Jordan Li: Quick check — do you have a preference for regions where you want Redwood nodes to live? you mentioned us-east-1 and eu-west-1 earlier.
[03:47] Maya Torres: Initially us-east-1 for latency to our core services, but we may want eu-west-1 for EU data residency. We also have a remote office in ap-southeast-1 but that's lower priority.
[03:58] Priya Raman: We can do a pilot in us-east-1 and bring up a eu-west-1 replica for residency testing. Note that cross-region calls introduce latency and potentially egress costs if traffic crosses clouds. For best performance keep model serving in the same region as the request origin.
[04:17] Samir Patel: Any difference in private endpoint support across clouds? We use both AWS and GCP.
[04:23] Priya Raman: Implementation details differ but capability is the same: AWS PrivateLink, GCP Private Service Connect, and Azure Private Link are supported with equivalent guarantees. We'll share exact steps per cloud.
[04:36] Maya Torres: Regarding management plane: can we lock the control plane down to talk only to a set of IPs? Our policy wants only corporate IP ranges for management traffic.
[04:46] Carlos Mendes: In Private deployments yes — control plane endpoints can be fronted by private endpoints in your VPC and you can configure allowlists. For hosted control plane there's a managed IP list but that won't satisfy strict no-external-eval policies. Private-mode is the right fit for you.
[05:05] Evan Brooks: Ok. How would onboarding look? We want a small pilot: 2 GPU nodes, a test model, and run a perf test against a canned prompt set.
[05:14] Priya Raman: Typical pilot: we provision a dedicated fleet or customer VPC deployment in your account, set up peering or private endpoints, validate egress, and run a one-day benchmark with your prompts. We'll instrument latency and cost. We'll share terraform snippets to stand up the infra.
[05:29] Samir Patel: On the perf tests — are you able to stream tokens? we need streaming for low-latency interactive use-cases.
[05:36] Priya Raman: Yes, streaming is supported. We'll also show how to configure batching vs single-request to tune latency/cost tradeoffs.
[05:45] Lena Chu: KMS integration—do you support customer-managed keys? we require keys under our account for secrets and model artifacts.
[05:52] Carlos Mendes: Yes, KMS/HSM integrations are supported. You can bring your own key (BYOK) and we will encrypt artifacts at rest with it. We'll include KMS integration steps in the security doc.
[06:04] Maya Torres: A couple practical things: 1) we need to avoid overlapping CIDR; 2) we need to know what ports we must open; 3) we need a clear plan for failure modes (if peering drops, auto-fallback?).
[06:15] Jordan Li: Ports: generally we use TLS 443 for most control plane traffic; data plane for gRPC/HTTP is also over TLS ports. We'll provide the port list. For redundancy we recommend multi-az deployments and a fallback route to a different region/queue if peering fails — we can discuss SLOs for that.
[06:33] Samir Patel: Any special routing for KV cache replication? We have heavy session workloads and want to avoid cross-AZ chatty traffic.
[06:42] Priya Raman: Our runtime supports colocated KV caches per node and optional async replication. For high-throughput real-time apps we suggest co-locating serving nodes and cache in the same AZ and using regional replication only as backup to reduce cross-AZ egress.
[06:56] Maya Torres: About compliance: we need audit logs retained for at least 1 year and ability to export to our SIEM. Can Redwood push logs into our logging endpoints?
[07:05] Carlos Mendes: Yes, we can deliver audit logs to your S3/Kinesis/Cloud Logging endpoint over private endpoints. Log retention is configurable; we can also provide snapshots for audits.
[07:15] Evan Brooks: One last question on pricing: if we run dedicated reserved GPUs in our account versus Redwood-managed dedicated — does that change cost or SLA?
[07:25] Jordan Li: Two models: Dedicated reserved with Redwood-managed infra gives you SLA and simpler ops; customer-hosted Private reduces Redwood infra cost but shifts management to you. Pricing differs — we'll put a clear comparison in the follow-up.
[07:36] Maya Torres: Great. Let's talk timeline — we'd like to run a pilot in the first half of December if possible. Can you meet that?
[07:44] Priya Raman: Yes, if we get the VPC/CIDR info and DirectConnect details this week we can stand up a small pilot by early December.
[07:52] Jordan Li: Ok let's capture next steps. We'll send the peering cookbook, security artifacts, and terraform examples. Also propose a 30-45m network deep dive for your platform team next week.
[08:03] Samir Patel: Sounds good. Anything else from Redwood side?
[08:08] Carlos Mendes: We'll also include a checklist for no-internet-egress setups, and a short runbook for failover if a transit gateway attachment drops.
[08:17] Lena Chu: We'll try to get you an initial list of allowed destinations and the CIDR ranges by Thursday.
[08:23] Jordan Li: Perfect. Thanks everyone — we'll recap via email with links.
[08:28] (call ends, informal chatter)
